title: Little children (1 John 2:12–17)
hook: the elder writes tenderly to children, young people and elders

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old new commandment, and your line was walk in the light. What step did you take toward peace with someone? Day six hundred eighty-four.

Every family has its pet names. Kiddo. Sweetheart. Buddy. Some grandparents call grown adults by a childhood nickname until the end, and nobody minds, because it isn't about age. It's about belonging. The writer of First John has a pet name for his readers, and he uses it again and again: little children. It is almost his signature. In today's passage, he stops the flow of the letter and writes a little poem, a set of short lines addressed to everyone in the room, young and old. And then a warning about what can pull them away.

In the King James Bible: "I write unto you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one." And then he goes round the circle again: children, fathers, young men. Little children: you're forgiven. Fathers, the older ones: you have known him a long time. Young people: you are strong, the word of God lives in you, and you've already won a battle. Scholars aren't sure whether he means actual ages, or stages of faith, or whether all three are said to everyone at once. Maybe all three. Every reader is a little child who is forgiven, a mature one who knows, and a young one who is strong. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't write to scold. Every line begins with because: because you're forgiven, because you know, because you've overcome. He writes from what's already true of them. Then the warning: "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world." That can sound strange next to John's Gospel, where God so loved the world. But world here means something different: the way of life that leaves God out. He names it: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life." Wanting, looking, showing off. Appetite, envy, status. And he puts it in perspective: "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever." Trends pass. Love stays.
screen: then, large: `I WRITE UNTO YOU, LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a tender note, in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone younger than you, a child, a student, a new coworker, a younger sibling. Then someone older, a parent, a mentor, a neighbor. Then someone in the middle, a friend your own age. For each one, finish this sentence in your head: I'm writing to you because. Because you're forgiven. Because you've taught me. Because you're strong. Don't write what they should do. Write what's already true of them. If you pray, you can pray for each by name. The bell holds the time.
Little children. The elder's pet name for his readers: forgiven, belonging, written to because of what's already true.
Your line: little children. Today, send one of those three people a short note that begins, I'm writing because, and finish it with something true and kind. Day six hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Many Christian communities read 1 John 2:12–14 when welcoming new members or blessing children, young people and elders together, and the warning about the lust of the eyes and the pride of life is often used in teaching on simple living.

original.note: Greek: little children, a tender diminutive. used again and again in 1 John.

trapdoor: what you thought: a letter for kids.
what it means: a tender poem to everyone, young and old, built on what's already true of them, and a warning about what passes away.
what a scholar hears: teknia, an affectionate diminutive; and three groups that may be ages, stages of faith, or all of us at once.
